[00:00:25] Priya Shah: Totally, so for the POC we'll define success criteria up front. Text quality, hallucination rate, structured output format - those are the three big things. Do you have existing metrics you use internally?

[00:00:58] Luis Moreno: That's helpful. For automated scoring, we recommend a mix: exact-match checks for structured fields, semantic similarity for free-text (embedding cosine + threshold), and hallucination heuristics - e.g., hallucination if model asserts a diagnosis not present in the source.
[00:01:15] Dr. Nina Patel: How do you detect hallucinations automatically? There's always edge cases.
[00:01:22] Priya Shah: We use provenance checks: entity-level comparison between source notes and generated summary using NLP extraction. If an entity appears in the output but not in source, mark it as potential hallucination. We combine that with heuristics and sample-focused human review to validate false positives.
[00:01:39] Sam Reed: For acceptance thresholds, what do you usually see in healthcare pilots?
[00:01:45] Evan Carter: Typical threshold we propose: >= 90% pass rate on critical factual checks, <2% severe hallucination rate (meaning hallucinations that could change clinical decision), and structured-output exact match >=95% for fields like med list and dosages. These can be adjusted per your risk tolerance.
[00:02:03] Jordan Kim: The 95% structured match seems reasonable. For throughput, our daily volume in scope for pilot is about 15k notes, with average note length ~450 tokens. Peak QPS today is low but we want to validate scale.
[00:02:19] Luis Moreno: For the POC we typically run a benchmark set of ~10k prompts (diverse lengths) to capture latency tail and token cost. We can also run a targeted 200-sample human review set for high-quality scoring.
[00:02:34] Priya Shah: Suggested benchmark matrix: baseline model (hosted), quantized variant on Dedicated, and a fallback smaller model for cost comparison. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), and cost per 1k tokens.
[00:02:49] Dr. Nina Patel: Timeline? We have internal deadlines for vendor selection by the end of March.
[00:02:55] Evan Carter: Proposed pilot timeline: Week 0 (this week): confirm scope and sign pilot SOW. Week 1: data ingestion, golden prompt creation, baseline runs. Week 2: tune prompts, run automated regression tests and benchmark. Week 3: human evaluation on holdout set, hallucination analysis, format validation. Week 4: results review, final report and go/no-go recommendation. So, roughly 4 weeks.
[00:03:20] Jordan Kim: Does Redwood need PHI during the pilot? We prefer using de-identified data under a BAA.
[00:03:26] Priya Shah: We can support either approach. For PHI we require a BAA and Dedicated/Private deployment is recommended; otherwise de-identified S3 transfer over secure bucket works for hosted. We'll include our transfer checklist in the security packet.

[00:03:45] Priya Shah: Yes, our Private deployment supports customer-managed KMS and full audit logs. We'll attach architecture diagram and SOC2 docs.
[00:03:55] Sam Reed: Back to quality eval specifics - what should the golden prompt set look like?
[00:04:02] Luis Moreno: Golden prompts should include: 1) canonical clinical notes with expected summary outputs, 2) edge cases (abbreviations, negations), 3) adversarial examples prone to hallucination, and 4) structured extraction tests (med list, dosages). Aim for 300-500 golden prompts for regression; holdout 200 for human review.
[00:04:22] Dr. Nina Patel: We'll assemble a clinician-curated set for that. Will Redwood store the golden prompts?
[00:04:28] Priya Shah: We can either store them in a secured project bucket or you can keep them and execute the runs on your side - whichever you prefer for data governance.
[00:04:36] Evan Carter: On scoring: automated pass/fail rules for structured fields, embedding-based similarity >= 0.85 for free-text semantic match, and a human rating scale for clinical acceptability (1-5). Final score is weighted: 50% human avg, 30% automated factuality, 20% format/structured checks.
[00:04:56] Jordan Kim: How do you calibrate embedding thresholds - 0.85 seems high for clinical text with varying phrasing.
[00:05:02] Priya Shah: We usually pick thresholds using a small calibration set of 100 examples with human labels. We tune threshold to balance precision for factual matches, then run the larger automated pass.
[00:05:13] Dr. Nina Patel: We'll need a clear definition for hallucination severity levels.
[00:05:18] Luis Moreno: Agreed. We recommend taxonomy: minor (non-critical extra detail), moderate (could confuse clinician), severe (could change treatment). Automated detection flags likely candidates, but human adjudication required for final severity counts.
[00:05:34] Sam Reed: Format checks - our downstream systems require JSON with fields: summary_text, med_list[], diagnosis_codes[]. How strict should format validation be?
[00:05:42] Priya Shah: We enforce strict schema validation in the benchmark. Any deviation counts as a format failure and impacts the format score. We'll run JSON schema validation and field-level exact matches.

Benchmarks & Evaluation Plan (inline summary):
- Dataset: ~10k diverse notes for automated runs, 300-500 golden prompts for regression, 200 holdout for human review.
- Metrics: structured exact-match, embedding similarity for free-text (threshold calibrated), hallucination rate by severity, p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec throughput, cost per 1k tokens.
- Scoring: weighted composite = 50% human avg score (1-5), 30% automated factuality/pass-rate, 20% format/structured checks. Pass criteria: composite >= 0.9 OR meet individual thresholds (>=90% factual, <2% severe hallucinations, >=95% structured).
- Regression tests: run golden prompts on every model variant and store outputs; flag >5% drop in pass rate for manual review.
- Hallucination checks: entity provenance, negative/contradiction detection, assertion-of-unsupported-diagnoses flagged. Human adjudication defines final severity counts.
- Timeline: 4-week pilot as above.
